name: Erik Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and still junior on calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and I am slow when a bill has several changes. I earn above the usual rate because I take the late rota, not because I lead anyone. I do not use AI tools; I read the account and ask an experienced agent when the record is tangled.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Lila, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. She works regular hours at a clinic. We have about eight months of expenses saved, and several other centres are close enough for me to reach. I like getting a customer a real correction, but late calls make me miss the children’s supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves the calls mostly where they are. I would ask the shift to keep checking the bill history rather than trust a neat machine note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my late rota still pays, and eight months saved gives our family room if something breaks. I am still slow on mixed bills, so I cannot call my place entirely safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the late calls and ask an experienced agent to check one mixed bill with me each week. During the first year of small change, I’d keep the mortgage reserve intact and bring any wrong notes to the monthly staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about my own numbers, though not worried about AI taking the whole desk. My late-shift pay still depends on getting the bill right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill has tripped you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once missed a credit posted below the main charge. The customer called back, and I had to ask Sumi, the agent beside me, to find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise a wrong note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the wrong note to the staff meeting without the customer’s name. Others may have seen the same missed credit, and a shared list is more useful than my private grumble.

say: I’d tell the shift **calls remain** under a small change.
I’d ask agents to check **bill history** before sending machine notes.
think: I think my **late pay** continues for now.
I still worry about **slow mixed-bill work** despite eight months saved.
do: Keep **late calls** and ask for weekly account checks in 2026.
Bring **wrong notes** to the staff meeting during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about performance, less worried about AI.
S0.quote: My late-shift pay still depends on getting the bill right.
fieldNote: His **late-shift allowance** explains higher pay without senior standing.
He asks for **current-job coaching**, not a career course.
He uses a **staff meeting** to compare errors across agents.

steps.text: Keep late call shifts and check mixed bills with an experienced agent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take routine bill chats first, and the staff group should see the hour figures before management changes the late rota. I would ask for a paid route into the cases that remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose the late shifts that lift my pay even if the centre keeps me employed. Eight months saved buys search time, but Lila and I built our mortgage around both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join the staff group in asking for monthly paid-hour and error figures. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted billing role at a nearby centre only if the written hours and wage cover our mortgage, while keeping my current shifts until I sign an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Losing the late premium could hurt us before anybody says my job is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figure would the group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want hours by shift, not a count of answered customers. A floor can look busy while fewer agents are paid to be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a new course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for an AI course just to look willing. If an employer posts a funded training place for a paid billing job, I would read the terms with Lila before deciding.

say: I’d ask the **staff group** for paid-hour figures by shift.
I’d seek a **paid route** into remaining billing cases.
think: I fear losing the **late premium** before losing the job.
I know **eight months saved** cannot replace two mortgage wages forever.
do: Join a **group request** for hours and errors in 2026.
Seek **posted nearby billing work** with written mortgage-covering wages and hours; keep current shifts until I sign an offer.
S1.quote: Losing the late premium could hurt us before anybody says my job is gone.
fieldNote: He tracks **paid hours by shift**, not customer volume.
The **late premium** is material to the household mortgage.
He would compare **funded job terms** before any course commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the floor AGI by 2028 could handle calls and bill checks before the company has agreed what happens to us. I would ask the staff group to seek written notice and real paid vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think full thinking AI could take my late headset shifts in 2028. Robots arriving around 2031 do not delay that; eight months of savings protects us briefly, not until the children leave school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help the staff group put a notice request in writing and hold our savings for the mortgage. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid billing role with enough hours to cover the house, and take a funded course only if required for that named opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still make a plan. Eight months of savings is not eight months of a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Lila (my partner) not to spend the reserve on a kitchen refit. The cupboards are old, but the mortgage payment has a date on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would ask management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff group to send the same questions for every shift: notice, paid openings and how customers appeal wrong bills. A private meeting would leave the next shift in the dark.

say: I’d ask the **staff group** to secure written notice before 2028 calls move.
I’d demand **paid vacancies** before calls move to AGI.
think: I think **2028 AGI** could end my late headset shifts.
I see **eight months saved** as a short bridge, not a new wage.
do: Put a **group notice request** in writing and protect savings in 2026.
Apply for **posted paid billing work** after 2028 with mortgage-covering hours.
Take a **funded course** only if required for a named posted paid billing opening.
S2.quote: Eight months of savings is not eight months of a new job.
fieldNote: He correctly treats **2028 thinking AI** as his job deadline.
The family **defers a kitchen refit** to protect mortgage funds.
His **group request** includes a customer appeal route.

steps.text: Help staff group submit written notice and paid-vacancy questions
Delay the kitchen refit and preserve the mortgage reserve
Apply for posted paid billing work with mortgage-covering hours after 2028
Take funded billing course only if required for a named posted paid opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the staff group time to bargain for paid learning and real jobs before calls shrink. I would want a list of vacancies with wages, not a training poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could let me learn proper billing review if somebody pays me to study it. I still expect fewer call agents when AGI can reason through invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d help the group ask for a paid review course linked to a posted vacancy, and I’d complete it if the centre funds my time and names the job. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that posted paid review role only if its written hours and wage cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have time to ask for terms. A course without a paid billing-review opening is a poster, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training manager for the job posting, the hours and who pays for the study time. If those are written down, I could learn the new work slowly with support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep your current practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still ask an experienced agent to check mixed bills on my current shift. That is ordinary work practice, and it helps customers while the review course is being discussed.

say: I’d ask for **posted review jobs** with actual wages before anyone takes a course.
I’d seek **group bargaining** for paid learning before 2031.
think: I think I could learn **billing review** with funded time.
I still expect **fewer call agents** when AGI arrives.
do: Help request a **billing-review course** and complete it only with centre-funded paid study time for a named vacancy.
Apply for **posted paid review work** after 2031 at mortgage-covering hours.
S3.quote: A course without a paid billing-review opening is a poster, not a plan.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **current-job coaching** from a funded new-role course.
The course needs **paid time** and a named posted vacancy.
His move requires **written hours and wage** covering the mortgage.

steps.text: Join staff group request for paid review training linked to a posted vacancy
Complete billing-review course only with centre-funded paid study time for a named posted paid role
Apply for posted review work with written mortgage-covering hours and wage after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives the centre ten years to keep a paid route for junior agents and to show annual staffing numbers. I would ask the staff group to check the plan each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could become steadier at billing by 53 and still earn well on the late rota for years. Full thinking AI could remove those calls in 2036, while robots in 2039 come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the late calls, put part of each premium payment into savings and join the yearly staff meeting on paid hours. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid billing job if my calls end and its written wage and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, but the current wage and reserve give me room. A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to save without pretending the mortgage disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many late hours remain each year. If the premium falls early, Lila and I would revise the household budget before it becomes a missed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless we had a signed job offer and a workable journey. Several centres nearby mean we can look without moving first.

say: I’d request **annual staffing numbers** through the group as calls change.
I’d defend a **paid junior route** before 2036.
think: I think I could **improve billing skill** by 53.
I know **2036 thinking AI** may remove my late calls.
do: Keep **late calls**, save premium pay and attend staff hour meetings.
Seek **posted billing work** after 2036 if calls end and written wage and hours cover the mortgage.
S4.quote: A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to save without pretending the mortgage disappears.
fieldNote: His **late premium** may erode before complete job loss.
Nearby centres offer a **search option** without immediate moving costs.
He keeps the **children’s school** steady unless a signed offer justifies change.

steps.text: Keep late call shifts while the centre staffs them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My calls and account checks are thinking work, so robots in 2031 do not extend my wage. I would want a written staffing timetable, a group agreement on notice, and a posted paid role with enough hours to keep our mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how the company values a careful correction. A wrong bill left on a customer’s account can cost a family more than my extra five minutes.

headlineQuote: A wrong bill left on a customer’s account can cost a family more than my extra five minutes.
portrait: At **43**, Erik is a junior late-rota agent after secondary school, still slow on complex bills.
He earns **above usual pay** through late shifts and has eight months saved against a mortgage.
He avoids **AI tools** and asks experienced colleagues when account records are tangled.
He turns to **staff action** for notice and paid routes as screen work changes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his calls before an alternative wage protects the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **group notice agreement**, written staffing dates and a posted mortgage-covering role would help.
